arXiv:2608.02753v2 [cond-mat.str-el] 10 Aug 2026

Large scale neural quantum states reveal the interplay between superconductivity and quantum criticality in the Hofstadter-Hubbard model

Christopher Roth Affiliation: Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, 162 5th Avenue, New York, NY 10010, USA    Andrew Millis Affiliation: Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, 162 5th Avenue, New York, NY 10010, USA Affiliation: Department of Physics, Columbia University, New York, NY 10027, USA    Tomohiro Soejima (副島智大) Affiliation: Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, 162 5th Avenue, New York, NY 10010, USA Affiliation: Center for Quantum Phenomena, Department of Physics, New York University, 726 Broadway, New York, New York 10003, USA
Abstract

Understanding how a parent insulating state shapes the superconductivity that emerges upon doping is a long-standing problem dating back to Anderson’s resonating-valence-bond proposal. The triangular-lattice Hofstadter-Hubbard model with π/2\pi/2 flux per plaquette offers an ideal setting: at half filling it hosts two distinct parent states—an integer quantum Hall insulator and a chiral spin liquid—separated by a topological phase transition. Using neural quantum states on tori of up to 432432 sites, we present strong evidence that the transition is continuous, with a vanishing 2​e2e charge gap and critical charge fluctuations. Upon doping, we find a topological superconductor on either side of the transition. While the pairing order parameter remains nearly unchanged across the transition, the superfluid stiffness is strongly enhanced near the critical point. The energy scale of the superconductor is therefore set not by which parent state is doped, but by proximity to the transition between them. Our results establish neural quantum states as a powerful tool for understanding the interplay between unconventional electronic correlations and superconductivity.

In the early days following the discovery of high transition-temperature superconductivity in the copper-oxide materials, P.W. Anderson argued that there existed a class of remarkable insulating states, in which electrons were paired in such a way that if carrier motion were released by adding or removing electrons, superconductivity would result [1]. Subsequent work has added substantial theoretical perspective to Anderson’s original idea, including that the insulating states he intuited could be understood as quantum spin liquids [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. Despite this theoretical progress, there is limited knowledge about how the parent state affects the energy scales associated with superconductivity and thus influences the transition temperature.

An ideal model for understanding this interplay is realized by the Hofstadter-Hubbard model on the triangular lattice with π/2\pi/2 flux around each triangular plaquette. It is believed to host several different parent states at half filling—an integer quantum Hall state (IQH) with a band gap when the on-site interaction is weak, and a chiral spin liquid (CSL) [8] at intermediate coupling [9, 10, 11], and at very large UU a 120∘120^{\circ} antiferromagnet [12, 13]. Numerical studies suggest the phase transition between IQH and CSL is second order. The difference in Hall conductivity between the IQH and CSL phases implies the existence of gapless charged excitations at this critical point and a field theoretical analysis suggests the emergence of a topological superconductor upon doping [14].

Existing numerical studies on this problem find pairing of charged excitations [14], quasi-long-range order of the superconducting order parameter in quasi-1D [15, 16], large pairing susceptibility at low temperature [16], and nonzero superconducting order parameter [17]. However, the small system sizes or correlation lengths these methods can reach has limited their ability to access quantum critical physics, such as the existence of gapless excitations. Furthermore, these calculations have not estimated how the superconducting energy scales change throughout the phase diagram.

In this work, we use neural quantum states [18, 19, 20, 21] to accurately simulate large systems of up to 432432 sites. First, we resolve the quantum critical point between the IQH and CSL phases. We show that very large system sizes, accessible to date only with NQS methods, are required to observe the theoretically predicted vanishing of the 2​e2e charge gap and demonstrate the transition point is associated with critical charge fluctuations. Upon doping, we find a topological superconducting phase with off-diagonal long-range order (ODLRO) and nontrivial spin quantum Hall conductance. Near the critical point, charge fluctuations strongly enhance the superfluid stiffness, leading to increased superconducting coherence. In contrast, the pairing order parameter is largely unaffected by proximity to the critical point, suggesting the pair formation is not enhanced by quantum criticality. Thus, the behavior of the superconductor is governed less by which parent insulator is doped than by proximity to the transition between them. Our work establishes NQS as a uniquely viable tool for capturing phases with two-dimensional long-correlation-length fluctuations and resolving the interplay between superconductivity and quantum criticality.

Hamiltonian— We consider the triangular-lattice Hofstadter-Hubbard model with Φ=π/2\Phi=\pi/2 flux through each plaquette. We can choose a gauge such that all hoppings are imaginary:

H=i​t​∑i,jτi,j​ci†​cj+∑iUi​(ni↑−12)​(ni↓−12),H=it\sum_{i,j}\tau_{i,j}c^{\dagger}_{i}c_{j}+\sum_{i}U_{i}\Big(n_{i\uparrow}-\frac{1}{2}\Big)\Big(n_{i\downarrow}-\frac{1}{2}\Big), (1)

where τi​j=±1\tau_{ij}=\pm 1. The purely imaginary hoppings endow the model with S​O​(4)SO(4) symmetry at half filling [10, 14], generated from spin S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry and charge S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry [22, 23, 24, 25]. The Hamiltonian is particle-hole symmetric about half filling, so electron and hole dopings are equivalent. The details of the model are shown in App. A. At U=0U=0, the ground state at half filling is an integer quantum Hall state with C=1C=1 per spin (Ctot=2C_{\rm tot}=2). As mentioned above, upon increasing UU, the model exhibits an IQH–CSL phase transition [9, 10, 11], and doping it can give rise to superconductivity [14, 15, 16, 17].

Hidden Fermion Pfaffian States— We train a variational wavefunction with the Hidden Fermion Pfaffian State (HFPS) architecture [26] to find the ground state of the Hofstadter-Hubbard model. This wavefunction, which introduces hidden fermions in order to learn correlation on top of a mean field fermion state, has been used to understand superconductivity in the t−t′t-t^{\prime} square lattice Hubbard model [27] as well as t-J bilayers [28]. Here we use a residual convolutional neural network architecture [29] to parameterize the couplings between electrons and hidden fermions. The pairing orbitals for the visible fermions are chosen to be block-circulant such that the wavefunction has the underlying translational symmetry of the Hamiltonian. Therefore, we can compute a translationally symmetric wavefunction with only a single Pfaffian evaluation, and we can efficiently scale to large system sizes. We consider C6C_{6} symmetric clusters of size 3​L×3​L\sqrt{3}L\times\sqrt{3}L with periodic boundary conditions. Simulations were performed using the Quantax [30] package, which uses lrux [31] to accelerate the computation of determinants and pfaffians. The network and training procedure are described in detail in App. E.1.

Vanishing charge gap—

We first show that our variational ansatz can correctly capture the two gapped phases. We use the following flux-threading procedure to measure the Hall conductance and the spin quantum Hall conductance [32, 9, 33]. We find the variational ground state at U=10U=10 and U=16U=16 at different values of charge and spin flux. By computing the evolution of many-body polarization with charge/spin flux, we obtain σx​yc=2​e2h,σx​ys=2​ℏ8​π\sigma_{xy}^{c}=2\frac{e^{2}}{h},\sigma_{xy}^{s}=2\frac{\hbar}{8\pi} at U=10U=10, and σx​yc=0,σx​ys=2​ℏ8​π\sigma_{xy}^{c}=0,\sigma_{xy}^{s}=2\frac{\hbar}{8\pi} at U=16U=16, consistent with IQH and CSL phases, respectively (see App. B).

By tuning UU to the critical point, our variational ansatz shows a vanishing 2​e2e charge gap. In Fig. 2(a) we show the 2​e2e charge gap at different system sizes. The solid lines show our estimate of the 2​e2e charge gap using our variational wavefunctions at Ne=NsiteN_{e}=N_{\mathrm{site}} and Ne=Nsite−2N_{e}=N_{\mathrm{site}}-2 and the dashed lines show the result of a zero-variance extrapolation as described in App. E.2. The difference between the raw and extrapolated energies is very small, showing that our variational ansatz likely captures the energy gap to good accuracy.

As system size increases the minimum value of the 2​e2e gap trends toward zero and shifts from U≈12U\approx 12 to U≈13U\approx 13. On the 432432 site cluster, the smallest gap is at U=13.25U=13.25, and has a value of 0.22​t0.22t, roughly a factor of 2020 smaller than the band gap. This is in contrast to an earlier DMRG study that only found a ∼25%\sim 25\% decrease relative to the band gap [14].

Structure factor— The small-|𝒌||\boldsymbol{k}| behavior of the structure factor further reveals the nature of the critical point. Let us decompose the correlation function into an analytic part and a power-law part C⁡(x)=Canalytic​(x)+c​|x|−ηC(x)=C_{\rm analytic}(x)+c|x|^{-\eta}. Its Fourier transform at small |k||k| takes the form C⁡(k)=α​|k|2+β​|k|η−2C(k)=\alpha|k|^{2}+\beta|k|^{\eta-2} with a log correction when η=4\eta=4. Nonanalyticity of C⁡(k)C(k) as |k|→0|k|\to 0 therefore signals power-law decay of the correlation function. We consider the charge and spin structure factors Cn^​(𝐤)C_{\hat{n}}({\bf k}) and CS^z​(𝐤)C_{\hat{S}^{z}}({\bf k}) (see App. C), and fit the low-|𝒌||\boldsymbol{k}| data to a power law (Fig. 2(b)). While the spin structure factor always scales quadratically at small |𝐤||{\bf k}|, the charge structure factor has a much smaller scaling exponent near the critical point, signaling critical correlations.

Superconductivity upon doping— We next find that doping the Hofstadter-Hubbard model results in a topological superconductor, in agreement with theoretical and numerical predictions [14, 9, 16].

To capture superconductivity, we first establish the existence of off-diagonal long-range order. We consider nearest neighbor pairing of the form

Δ𝒙=112​2​∑⟨α,β⟩∈U𝒙phase​(α,β)​(cα,↑​cβ,↓−cα,↓​cβ,↑)\Delta_{\boldsymbol{x}}=\frac{1}{12\sqrt{2}}\sum_{\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle\in U_{\boldsymbol{x}}}\textrm{phase}(\alpha,\beta)(c_{\alpha,\uparrow}c_{\beta,\downarrow}-c_{\alpha,\downarrow}c_{\beta,\uparrow}) (2)

where ⟨α,β⟩∈U𝒙\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle\in U_{\boldsymbol{x}} includes all nearest neighbor bonds in a single magnetic unit cell centered at 𝐱{\bf x}, and the phases of these bonds are shown in the inset to Fig. 3(a). Here, as in Refs. [14, 15, 16, 17], we find the dominant pairing mode has 2​π2\pi winding about the rotational centers. ODLRO can be diagnosed by the correlator

Cp​(𝒓)=1N​∑𝐱⟨Δ𝐫+𝐱†​Δ𝐱⟩.C_{p}(\boldsymbol{r})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\bf x}\langle\Delta^{\dagger}_{\bf r+\bf x}\Delta_{\bf x}\rangle. (3)

In Fig. 3(a), we show the pair correlations Cp​(𝒓)C_{p}(\boldsymbol{r}) at U=8U=8 for different values of doping. The pair correlation function plateaus to a constant, indicating ODLRO.

The topological nature of the superconductor can be elucidated from spin quantum Hall conductivity. We compute this from flux-threading, analogously to the computation for IQH and CSL. In Fig. 3(b), we show the evolution of the many-body spin polarization Zxspin=exp⁡[4​π​i3​L​(X^↑−X^↓)]Z_{x}^{\rm spin}=\exp[\frac{4\pi i}{3L}(\hat{X}_{\uparrow}-\hat{X}_{\downarrow})] as we thread spin flux through the system. The polarization winds twice, consistent with spin quantum Hall conductivity σx​ys=2​ℏ8​π\sigma_{xy}^{s}=2\frac{\hbar}{8\pi}, in agreement with topological superconductivity predicted in the literature [14, 15, 16, 17].

Interplay of criticality and superconductivity—

We further characterize the pairing order parameter and superconducting stiffness. We compute the stiffness by threading flux ϕ\phi through the torus, and computing d2​Ed​ϕ2\frac{d^{2}E}{d\phi^{2}}, as we detail in App. D. The pairing order parameter is computed as Cp​(𝒓)\sqrt{C_{p}(\boldsymbol{r})} for |𝒓|>4|\boldsymbol{r}|>4.

We find that the stiffness is enhanced around the quantum critical point. In Fig. 4(a), we show the superfluid stiffness for various UU and doping levels. From the Nelson-Kosterlitz criterion [34], we estimate the transition temperature at U=13,δ=1/72U=13,\delta=1/72 to be 0.12​t0.12t, indicating a high transition temperature. At small doping, the stiffness is enhanced near the critical point of U∼13U\sim 13. The relative height of the peak diminishes as we increase doping.

A simple dimensional analysis can shed light on the peak of the stiffness [14]. The stiffness DsD_{s} has units of energy∼(length)−1\sim(\text{length})^{-1}. The doped problem has two length scales: δ−12\delta^{-\frac{1}{2}} and the correlation length of the parent state ξ\xi. Given ξ→∞\xi\to\infty at the critical point, we can fix the scaling form of the stiffness to be Ds=δ​F​(δξ)D_{s}=\sqrt{\delta}F\left(\frac{\sqrt{\delta}}{\xi}\right), where F⁡(0)=1F(0)=1, consistent with the scaling of the degeneracy temperature of free massless 2D boson gas. The functional form away from the critical point can be inferred from the degeneracy temperature of a massive 2D free boson gas, which goes as δm\frac{\delta}{m}. At small enough δ\delta, therefore, the stiffness peaks around the critical point.

In contrast, the pairing order parameter shows no feature at the quantum critical point. The order parameter peaks around U=6−7U=6-7, away from the critical point. This is consistent with pre-formed pairs, arising either from binding of electrons in the IQH phase [14, 16] or from anyon superconductivity from semions [2, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 41, 42], whose mobility peaks at the critical point.

Discussion— Our results demonstrate the power of neural quantum states to understand the physics of topological quantum phase transitions. By accessing large system sizes with an expressive variational ansatz we uncovered properties of critical phases at scales beyond what is achievable with other numerical methods.

The systematic decrease of the 2​e2e charge gap with system size and the power-law form of the charge structure factor are consistent with a conformally invariant quantum critical point. Our diagnostics, however, do not determine critical exponents, verify z=1z=1 scaling, or match the operator content against candidate field theories [43, 44, 45]. Developing techniques that extract such universal data from critical variational wavefunctions is an important direction for future work.

Our observation of an enhanced superfluid stiffness around the quantum critical point suggests critical charge fluctuations of the parent state stabilize the superconductor. Considering that the pairing order parameter does not show a similar enhancement, we posit that the critical fluctuations enhance superconductivity by promoting pair mobility. Surprisingly, despite the differences in how the superconductor forms upon doping the IQH and the CSL, the phenomenological behavior is remarkably similar on either side of the critical point. This suggests that doping near a quantum phase transition [14, 46] may provide a more favorable route to strong superconductivity than doping a parent insulating phase.

An experimental realization of this model may be achieved either in a cold-atom system [47], or in moiré systems [48, 9]. The high superconducting transition temperatures relative to the bare kinetic energy scale make this an ideal system for exploring the physics of strongly correlated superconductors.

Appendix A Geometry and gauge choice

Our simulations are performed on 3​L×3​L\sqrt{3}L\times\sqrt{3}L lattices on a torus geometry shown in Fig. 5 as done in Refs. [50, 51], for L=8,10,12L=8,10,12. This can be constructed starting from an L×LL\times L triangular lattice on a torus with lattice vectors {3/2,3/2}\{3/2,\sqrt{3}/2\} and {0,3}\{0,\sqrt{3}\}. From this, the 3​L×3​L\sqrt{3}L\times\sqrt{3}L lattice is formed by placing three sites in each unit cell, displaced from the unit-cell origin by {0,0}\{0,0\}, {1/2,3/2}\{1/2,\sqrt{3}/2\}, and {1,3}\{1,\sqrt{3}\}. This lattice maintains D6D_{6} symmetry, and the shortest loops around the torus now traverse the next-nearest neighbor direction.

We choose a C6C_{6} symmetric gauge as done in [14, 9], which has a 2×22\times 2 unit cell with 12 bonds. A diagram of the Hamiltonian is shown in Fig. 6. The arrows represent kinetic hopping of i​tit. Due to hermiticity the hopping sign is −i​t-it in the opposite direction of the arrows. This unit cell has 4 sites and 12 bonds, and is therefore tiled 3​L2/43L^{2}/4 times in order to form the 3​L×3​L\sqrt{3}L\times\sqrt{3}L lattice.

Appendix B Identifying the IQH and CSL phases from flux threading

The IQH and CSL can be distinguished by their response to flux threading, which measures the Hall response to an applied field.

Our real space torus is spanned by two basis vectors

𝑳1=L⁡(0,3),𝑳2=L⁡(32,32).\boldsymbol{L}_{1}=L(0,\sqrt{3}),\quad\boldsymbol{L}_{2}=L\left(\frac{3}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right). (4)

We thread the flux in the yy direction:

e​𝑨=(0,Φy​13​L)⟹𝑳1⋅e​𝑨=Φy,𝑳2⋅e​𝑨=Φy2.e\boldsymbol{A}=\left(0,\Phi_{y}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}L}\right)\implies\boldsymbol{L}_{1}\cdot e\boldsymbol{A}=\Phi_{y},\quad\boldsymbol{L}_{2}\cdot e\boldsymbol{A}=\frac{\Phi_{y}}{2}. (5)

Many-body polarization is measured using the phase of the operator exp⁡[i​𝑮⋅𝑹^]\exp[i\boldsymbol{G}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{R}}], where 𝑮\boldsymbol{G} is a reciprocal lattice vector of the torus and 𝑹^\hat{\boldsymbol{R}} is the position operator. For our torus, the reciprocal lattice is spanned by the basis vectors

𝑮1=4​π3​3​L​(32,−32),𝑮2=4​π3​L​(1,0).\boldsymbol{G}_{1}=\frac{4\pi}{3\sqrt{3}L}\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},-\frac{3}{2}\right),\boldsymbol{G}_{2}=\frac{4\pi}{3L}(1,0). (6)

We measure the many-body polarization using 𝑮2\boldsymbol{G}_{2}:

Px=3​L4​π​Im⁡log⁡⟨exp⁡[4​π​i3​L​X^]⟩≡3​L4​π​Im⁡log⁡⟨Zx⟩,P_{x}=\frac{3L}{4\pi}\operatorname{Im}\log\braket{\exp\left[\frac{4\pi i}{3L}\hat{X}\right]}\equiv\frac{3L}{4\pi}\operatorname{Im}\log\braket{Z_{x}}, (7)

where X^=∑𝒓rx​n^𝒓\hat{X}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{r}}r_{x}\hat{n}_{\boldsymbol{r}}.

Let us now compute the Hall conductance. We first compute the current density from the time derivative of the polarization:

jx=1Area​d​Pxd​t=23​3​L2​3​L4​π​d⁡(Im⁡log⁡⟨exp⁡[4​π​i3​L​X^]⟩)d​Φy​d​Φyd​t=13​L​W×d​Φyd​tj_{x}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{Area}}\frac{dP_{x}}{dt}=\frac{2}{3\sqrt{3}L^{2}}\frac{3L}{4\pi}\frac{d(\operatorname{Im}\log\braket{\exp\left[\frac{4\pi i}{3L}\hat{X}\right]})}{d\Phi_{y}}\frac{d\Phi_{y}}{dt}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}L}W\times\frac{d\Phi_{y}}{dt} (8)

where W=(Px​(Φy=2​π)−Px​(Φy=0))/2​πW=(P_{x}(\Phi_{y}=2\pi)-P_{x}(\Phi_{y}=0))/2\pi is the winding number of the threading process. On the other hand, the electric field is given by 𝑬=d​𝑨d​t=13​L​d​Φyd​t\boldsymbol{E}=\frac{d\boldsymbol{A}}{dt}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}L}\frac{d\Phi_{y}}{dt}. Combining these, we get

jx=W​E⟹σ=e2h​W.j_{x}=WE\implies\sigma=\frac{e^{2}}{h}W. (9)

We can similarly measure response to a spin flux by writing

e​𝑨sσ=σ⁡(0,Φy​13​L),Pxσ=3​L4​π​Im​log⁡⟨exp⁡[4​π​i3​L​(X^↑−X^↓)]⟩≡3​L4​π​Im​log⁡⟨Zxspin⟩.e\boldsymbol{A}_{s}^{\sigma}=\sigma\left(0,\Phi_{y}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}L}\right),\quad P_{x}^{\sigma}=\frac{3L}{4\pi}\operatorname{Im}\log\braket{\exp\left[\frac{4\pi i}{3L}(\hat{X}_{\uparrow}-\hat{X}_{\downarrow})\right]}\equiv\frac{3L}{4\pi}\operatorname{Im}\log\braket{Z^{\rm spin}_{x}}. (10)

The same algebra as for the charge Hall conductivity gives us

σx​ys=ℏ8​π​Ws.\sigma_{xy}^{s}=\frac{\hbar}{8\pi}W^{s}. (11)

In Fig. 7 we show the Hall response to charge and spin flux for U=10U=10 and U=16U=16. For U<UcU<U_{c} we have two copies of an IQH formed by the up and down spins, so under flux threading the up and down spins are moved independently. The charge and spin quantum Hall responses should then show winding numbers W=Ws=2W=W^{s}=2, as is clearly observed at U=10U=10.

In contrast, for U>UcU>U_{c} we expect that the charge is localized, and we should no longer see a winding of the charge many-body polarization under flux threading. As expected for the CSL phase, we only see a spin response at U=16U=16.

Appendix C Detecting quantum criticality through structure factors

C.1 Structure factor and quantum criticality

For an operator O^\hat{O}, we define the connected spatial correlation function as follows:

CO^​(𝐫)=1N​∑𝐱[⟨O^𝐱+𝐫†​O^𝐱⟩−⟨O^𝐱+𝐫⟩​⟨O^𝐱⟩].C_{\hat{O}}({\bf r})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\bf x}\Big[\langle{\hat{O}}^{\dagger}_{\bf x+\bf r}{\hat{O}_{\bf x}}\rangle-\langle{\hat{O}}_{\bf x+\bf r}\rangle\langle{\hat{O}}_{\bf x}\rangle\Big]. (12)

For phases with long range order, CO^​(𝐫)C_{\hat{O}}({\bf r}) should be non-zero as |𝐫|→∞|{\bf r}|\rightarrow\infty, while in most other cases it falls off exponentially. The exception is quantum critical phases where CO^​(𝐫)∼1/|𝐫|ηC_{\hat{O}}({\bf r})\sim 1/|{\bf r}|^{\eta} at large |𝐫||{\bf r}|. In order to distinguish a power law from an exponential, one must determine whether log⁡(CO^​(𝐫))\log(C_{\hat{O}}({\bf r})) decays linearly or super-linearly with log⁡(|𝐫|)\log(|{\bf r}|). However, in practice it is hard to fit a long-range correlation tail from Monte Carlo data, as the statistical noise dominates at large |𝐫||{\bf r}| and causes the sign of the correlation function to oscillate.

To ameliorate this problem, we consider correlation functions in momentum space, often called structure factors,

CO^​(𝐤)=∑𝐫ei​𝐤⋅𝐫​CO^​(𝐫).C_{\hat{O}}({\bf k})=\sum_{\bf r}e^{i{\bf k}\cdot{\bf r}}C_{\hat{O}}({\bf r}). (13)

For each value of |𝐤||{\bf k}|, CO^​(𝐤)C_{\hat{O}}({\bf k}) contains a sum over NN terms which improves the statistical signal by N\sqrt{N}—this improves the resolution by a factor of 10–20 on the system sizes we study. Furthermore, CO^​(𝐤)C_{\hat{O}}({\bf k}) is positive semidefinite, and thus taking the logarithm is unproblematic.

For a phase with long range order, CO^​(𝐤)C_{\hat{O}}({\bf k}) should scale extensively with system size. On the other hand, for exponentially decaying correlations, CO^​(𝐤)C_{\hat{O}}({\bf k}) should be analytic at |𝐤|=0|{\bf k}|=0 and therefore must scale quadratically at small |𝐤||{\bf k}|: CO^​(𝐤)−CO^​(𝐤=0)∼|𝐤|2C_{\hat{O}}({\bf k})-C_{\hat{O}}({\bf k}=0)\sim|{\bf k}|^{2}.

However, if CO^​(𝐫)C_{\hat{O}}({\bf r}) follows a power law with η>2\eta>2, the structure factor can be non-analytic at 𝐤=0{\bf k}=0, where the small-|𝐤||{\bf k}| scaling goes as CO^​(𝐤)∼α​|𝐤|2+β​|𝐤|η−2C_{\hat{O}}({\bf k})\sim\alpha|{\bf k}|^{2}+\beta|{\bf k}|^{\eta-2}. Therefore, by examining the small-|𝐤||{\bf k}| behavior of the structure factor we can identify critical fluctuations.

C.2 Kinetic energy fluctuations

In the main text Fig. 2 we present evidence that there are critical charge fluctuations in the vicinity of the QCP. Here we show that there are critical kinetic energy fluctuations as well, which persist to finite doping. First, we define the local kinetic energy operator,

T^𝐱=i​sign​(𝜹)​∑σ=↑,↓(c^†𝐱+𝜹/𝟐,σ​c^𝐱−𝜹/𝟐,σ−c^†𝐱−𝜹/𝟐,σ​c^𝐱+𝜹/𝟐,σ),{\hat{T}}_{\bf x}=i\ \textrm{sign}(\boldsymbol{\delta})\sum_{\sigma=\uparrow,\downarrow}({\hat{c}^{\dagger}}_{\bf x+\boldsymbol{\delta}/2,\sigma}{\hat{c}}_{\bf x-\boldsymbol{\delta}/2,\sigma}-{\hat{c}^{\dagger}}_{\bf x-\boldsymbol{\delta}/2,\sigma}{\hat{c}}_{\bf x+\boldsymbol{\delta}/2,\sigma}), (14)

where 𝜹\boldsymbol{\delta} is a nearest-neighbor lattice displacement and sign​(𝜹)\textrm{sign}(\boldsymbol{\delta}) are the signs shown in Fig. 6. Again we look at the small-|𝐤||{\bf k}| behavior of the structure factor CT^​(𝐤)C_{\hat{T}}({\bf k}). Unlike the charge structure factor, here CT^​(𝐤=𝟎)≠0C_{\hat{T}}({\bf k}={\bf 0})\neq 0. Therefore we find it is best to fit the small-|𝐤||{\bf k}| behavior with a quadratic function, CT^​(𝐤)∼c0+c1​|𝐤|+c2​|𝐤|2C_{\hat{T}}({\bf k})\sim c_{0}+c_{1}|{\bf k}|+c_{2}|{\bf k}|^{2}. Any linear component indicates that CT^​(𝐤)C_{\hat{T}}({\bf k}) is non-analytic at 𝐤=0{\bf k}=0. In the left panel of Fig. 8, we plot the linear coefficient of the fit, c1c_{1}, as a function of UU at half filling. This component is zero deep in the insulator phase but becomes strongly negative around the critical point, signaling critical fluctuations. In the right panel of Fig. 8, the behavior of the energy structure-factor fit at finite doping is shown. The peak in the |𝐤||{\bf k}|-linear component decreases as a function of doping until it is undetectable at δ∼0.1\delta\sim 0.1. This, in conjunction with the superfluid stiffness in main text Fig. 4, gives evidence that the critical point remains influential until about 10%10\% doping.

C.3 Fits to structure factors

In this section we show details of the fits to the small |𝐤||{\bf k}| behavior of the charge and energy structure factors. The charge structure factor is 00 at 𝐤=𝟎{\bf k}={\bf 0} and positive definite, therefore we can fit the low-|𝐤||{\bf k}| behavior to a power law. The results for U=4U=4, which is deep in the IQH phase, U=13.25U=13.25, which is near the critical point, and U=20U=20, which is deep in the CSL phase, are shown in Fig. 9(a). For these calculations we fit |𝐤|<π/3|{\bf k}|<\pi/3, as beyond these values the higher-order contributions to the structure factors of the insulators become relevant. However, as seen by the orange curve, the fit around the critical point persists to much larger |𝐤||{\bf k}|.

Fitting the kinetic energy fluctuations is trickier as CT^​(𝐤=0)C_{\hat{T}}({\bf k}=0) is generically non-zero as it represents the variance of the kinetic energy 11 1 To avoid confusion, we note that the variance of the total energy is zero for an eigenstate but the variance of the kinetic energy can still be finite.. Therefore, we would like to fit the data to the functional form CT^​(𝐤)=α​|𝐤|2+β​|𝐤|η−2+γC_{\hat{T}}({\bf k})=\alpha|{\bf k}|^{2}+\beta|{\bf k}|^{\eta-2}+\gamma. In practice we find that fixing η=3\eta=3 works quite well. The fits to the energy structure factor for the IQH, QCP, and CSL are shown in Fig. 9(b). As seen by the orange curve, there is sub-quadratic behavior at U=13.25U=13.25 although there is a slight deviation from linear behavior at small-|𝐤||{\bf k}| points.

Appendix D Superfluid stiffness

D.1 Extraction of superfluid stiffness and BKT transition temperature

We compute the superconducting stiffness from flux response. As defined in App. B, the flux ϕy\phi_{y} enters as a uniform vector potential e​𝑨=(0,ϕy3​L)e\boldsymbol{A}=\left(0,\frac{\phi_{y}}{\sqrt{3}L}\right). The superfluid weight in the yy direction is the curvature of the ground-state energy per unit area with respect to AyA_{y} [52],

Ds=1𝒜​∂2E∂Ay2|Ay=0,D_{s}=\frac{1}{\mathcal{A}}\frac{\partial^{2}E}{\partial A_{y}^{2}}\bigg|_{A_{y}=0}, (15)

where 𝒜=|𝑳1×𝑳2|=3​32​L2\mathcal{A}=|\boldsymbol{L}_{1}\times\boldsymbol{L}_{2}|=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}L^{2} is the area of the torus. Using ∂2E∂ϕy2=13​L2​∂2E∂Ay2\frac{\partial^{2}E}{\partial\phi_{y}^{2}}=\frac{1}{3L^{2}}\frac{\partial^{2}E}{\partial A_{y}^{2}}, we obtain

Ds=23​d2​Ed​ϕy2.D_{s}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\frac{d^{2}E}{d\phi_{y}^{2}}. (16)

Since the condensate carries charge 2​e2e, the phase stiffness of the pairing order parameter is ρspair=Ds/4\rho_{s}^{\rm pair}=D_{s}/4, and the Nelson-Kosterlitz universal jump condition [34] ρspair​(TBKT)=2π​kB​TBKT\rho_{s}^{\rm pair}(T_{\rm BKT})=\frac{2}{\pi}k_{B}T_{\rm BKT} yields an upper bound on the transition temperature,

kB​TBKT≲π2​ρspair=π8​Ds.k_{B}T_{\rm BKT}\lesssim\frac{\pi}{2}\rho_{s}^{\rm pair}=\frac{\pi}{8}D_{s}. (17)

D.2 Extracting stiffness from finite difference

Assuming that the ground-state energy is quadratic in flux near ϕy=0\phi_{y}=0, Eq. (16) may be approximated using a finite difference method on the larger systems,

Ds=43​E⁡(ϕy=ϕs)−E⁡(ϕy=0)ϕs2,D_{s}=\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}\frac{E(\phi_{y}=\phi_{s})-E(\phi_{y}=0)}{\phi_{s}^{2}}, (18)

where we set ϕs=0.4×2​π\phi_{s}=0.4\times 2\pi. This greatly reduces computational time as it only involves training the model at two flux values.

To verify the accuracy of this method, we confirmed that E⁡(ϕy)E(\phi_{y}) is a quadratic function, and that Eq. (18) reproduces a quadratic fit to good accuracy. In Fig. 10 we show a fit to E⁡(ϕy)E(\phi_{y}) as a function of ϕy\phi_{y} at U=8,δ=1/8U=8,\delta=1/8, showing a clear quadratic behavior. In Table 1, we compare the stiffness extracted via the quadratic fit on ϕy=2​π×{0,0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4}\phi_{y}=2\pi\times\{0,0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4\} versus Eq. (18) at representative points corresponding to doping the IQH, QCP, and CSL. The two calculations show good agreement.

D.3 Finite size effects of superfluid stiffness

In Fig. 10(b) the superfluid stiffness is shown on the 192192 and 432432 site clusters at δ=1/24\delta=1/24 as a function of UU. Away from UcU_{c} the superfluid stiffness is approximately size invariant, but around the critical point the stiffness has a larger peak for the N=432N=432 site system. This is consistent with the energy gap, which decreases and moves to larger UU as system size is increased.

Appendix E Details of variational optimization

E.1 Hyperparameters and training procedure

For all of the calculations a hidden fermion Pfaffian state wavefunction [26] was used in conjunction with a residual convolutional neural network (R-CNN) with 3636 features, 88 layers and 88 hidden fermions. The visible-visible couplings have a 2×22\times 2 sublattice structure such that they have the same unit cell as the Hamiltonian couplings.

A separate calculation was done for each doping level, system size, and flux threading, while we used transfer learning to compute the ground state as UU is varied. We first trained at U=4U=4 before adiabatically increasing UU and making sure the calculation was converged at each step.

First, we optimized the mean field on the Hubbard model at U=3U=3 with a pinning field consistent with the order parameter shown in the inset of Fig. 3(a).

Hmf=i​t​∑i,jτi,j​ci†​cj+∑iUi​ni↑​ni↓+μ​∑i,σni,σ+Δ​∑⟨α,β⟩phase​(α,β)​(cα,↑​cβ,↓−cα,↓​cβ,↑)H_{\rm mf}=it\sum_{i,j}\tau_{i,j}c^{\dagger}_{i}c_{j}+\sum_{i}U_{i}n_{i\uparrow}n_{i\downarrow}+\mu\sum_{i,\sigma}n_{i,\sigma}+\Delta\sum_{\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle}\textrm{phase}(\alpha,\beta)(c_{\alpha,\uparrow}c_{\beta,\downarrow}-c_{\alpha,\downarrow}c_{\beta,\uparrow}) (19)

as done in Ref. [27]. For all calculations we use Δ=0.2\Delta=0.2. We find that adding the pinning field to the mean field starting point substantially improves the convergence as well as the energy after a fixed number of iterations. We show the energy after 10001000 training iterations for two different doping levels at Δ=0,0.2\Delta=0,0.2 in Table 2.

We find that after 10001000 iterations the wavefunction without pinning has still not found the correct superconducting order, explaining the much higher energy.

E.2 Zero-variance extrapolation

Throughout this work we compute gaps by considering the difference in energy between two eigenstates. Furthermore, the superfluid stiffness is computed from the dependence of the ground-state energy on the threaded flux. Thus, the error in these results is set by the error scale of the variational energies.

In order to estimate the error in the variational energy, we perform a zero-variance extrapolation [53, 29], using two states: the raw wavefunction computed using a CNN, and the wavefunction after C6C_{6} + spin-inversion projection.

⟨𝐧|ψsymm⟩=∑g∈Gχg​⟨g​𝐧|ψ⟩\langle{\bf n}|\psi_{\rm symm}\rangle=\sum_{g\in G}\chi_{g}\langle g{\bf n}|\psi\rangle (20)

where GG is the group containing C6C_{6} rotations as well as a spin inversion operation, and g​𝐧g{\bf n} is the transformation of the Fock state 𝐧{\bf n} by gg. Here we find the lowest possible |ψsymm⟩|\psi_{\rm symm}\rangle by trying all possible characters χg\chi_{g}. For the doping levels we consider, where the number of holes is always even, the eigenvalue under a π/3\pi/3 rotation is exp⁡(i​π3​(4+N−Ne2))\exp\Big(i\frac{\pi}{3}\big(4+\frac{N-N_{e}}{2}\big)\Big), while under spin parity it is exp⁡(i​π​N−Ne2)\exp\Big(i\pi\frac{N-N_{e}}{2}\Big). Once we have obtained |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle and |ψsymm⟩|\psi_{\rm symm}\rangle the extrapolated energy is computed as

Eext=Esymm+Esymm−Eσsymm2−σ2​σsymm2.E_{\rm ext}=E_{\rm symm}+\frac{E_{\rm symm}-E}{\sigma^{2}_{\rm symm}-\sigma^{2}}\sigma^{2}_{\rm symm}. (21)

In Fig. 11 we show approximate energy errors using this extrapolation procedure. Here we see that the energy errors are fairly small both at half filling and with hole doping.

E.3 Numerical Resources

The data shown in this paper required approximately 10510^{5} hours on NVIDIA H200 GPUs. In Table 3 the approximate time needed for 20002000 training iterations at half filling is shown as a function of system size.

Upon hole doping, the computation becomes slightly cheaper due to the smaller Pfaffian in the output layer.
